title: Head injury: warning signs of a serious problem
asks: hit my head how do I know if it is serious
he got knocked out for a minute is that bad
kid fell and hit head what do I watch for
when is a head injury an emergency
clear fluid or blood from ear after a fall
hit hed feel dizzy and sick
pupils different sizes after hitting head
should I let him sleep after a head injury
answer: If a head injury is suspected, seek immediate medical attention. Suspect a traumatic brain injury if any of these appear: a deteriorating level of consciousness; double vision; increased restlessness, combative or agitated behavior; repeated vomiting; seizures; weakness or tingling in the arms or legs; a severe or worsening headache.

Other signs to look for: nausea and vomiting, convulsions or twitches, slurred speech, confusion and loss of memory (do they know who they are, where they are, what day it is?), recent unconsciousness, dizziness, drowsiness, blurred vision, unequal pupils, black eyes, paralysis, headache, a dent or swelling of the head, staggering while walking.
Clear fluid or blood leaking from the nose or ears can indicate a more severe injury: treat it as an emergency. An open head injury (a break in the skull) is a medical emergency.
Prolonged loss of consciousness, altered thinking or combativeness after a blow to the head can mean bleeding in the brain and may progress to death: evacuate the person immediately.
Symptoms can occur immediately after the injury or develop gradually over time. Most concussions happen without the person losing consciousness.
Keep checking the person's level of consciousness and orientation. Wake them frequently, even during sleeping periods, to check.
warnings: A person with blunt trauma to the head should be treated as though they also have a spinal injury: do not move them until the head and neck are stabilized, unless they are in immediate danger.
Do not give a person with a head injury anything to eat or drink.
Pain medication that depresses the central nervous system can further complicate a head injury.
Do not try to remove an object sticking out of the head.

Open skull wound: do not put pressure on the wound, do not push brain matter back, and do not remove or disturb anything in the wound. Cover it with a loose, moistened dressing, keep the head higher than the body, keep the person warm and seek medical assistance immediately.

quotes.text: It is crucial to seek immediate medical attention if a head injury is suspected, as prompt evaluation and treatment are essential to prevent further complications.

A traumatic brain injury should be suspected if the casualty exhibits any of the following signs: • A deteriorating level of consciousness. • Experiencing double vision. • Exhibiting increased restlessness, combative, or agitated behavior. • Repeated vomiting. • Positive results from a structural brain injury detection device, if available. • Seizures. • Weakness or tingling sensations in the arms or legs. • Severe or worsening headache.

The signs and symptoms that a first aid provider might observe are: • Nausea and vomiting. • Convulsions or twitches. • Slurred speech. • Confusion and loss of memory. (Do they know who they are? Do they know where they are? Do they know what day it is?). • Recent unconsciousness. • Dizziness. • Drowsiness. • Blurred vision, unequal pupils, or bruising (black eyes). • Paralysis (partial or full). • Complaint of headache. • Bleeding or other fluid discharge from the scalp, nose, or ears. • Deformity of the head (depression or swelling). • Staggering while walking.
Clear fluid or blood drainage. Leakage of clear fluid (cerebrospinal fluid) or blood from the nose, ears, or wound can indicate a more severe injury and should be treated as an emergency.
Open head injuries are considered medical emergencies. If an open head injury is suspected, it is crucial to seek immediate medical attention for evaluation, diagnosis, and appropriate treatment.

Trauma sufficient to cause prolonged loss of consciousness usually produces such lesions. Clinically this may present as specific cranial nerve findings such as a gaze preference. Dependent on the location, though, this may also present with altered mentation and combativeness, and may even progress to death. EVACUATE THE PATIENT TO THE PHYSICIAN IMMEDIATELY.
Contusions can also involve hemorrhages of the brain that result from the mechanical forces that move the hemispheres of the brain relative to the skull.

It is important to seek medical attention if any of these signs are present after a head injury, as they can indicate a range of severity from a mild concussion to more serious brain trauma. The above symptoms can occur immediately after the injury or may develop gradually over time.

The primary characteristic of a concussion is a temporary disruption of brain function. Concussions may not always involve a loss of consciousness. In fact, most concussions occur without a person losing consciousness.

It is important to continually assess the patient's level of consciousness and orientation along with the ability to respond to verbal commands. These parameters are indications of the higher functions controlled in the cranial cavity. When there is a head injury, swelling or bleeding in the brain may impair the ability to verbally respond and may result in increased drowsiness and depressed respirations. The patient needs to be awakened frequently, even during sleeping periods to assess the level of consciousness. Administering pain medication that is a central nervous system depressant can further complicate the patient's condition.

Casualties with blunt trauma should be treated as though they also have a spinal injury. The casualty should not be moved until the head and neck are stabilized unless they are in immediate danger (such as close to a burning vehicle).
The first aid provider should not attempt to remove a protruding object from the head or give the casualty anything to eat or drink.
DO NOT attempt to put unnecessary pressure on the wound or attempt to push any brain matter back into the head (skull). DO NOT apply pressure dressing.

In severe head injuries where brain tissue is protruding, leave the wound alone. Carefully place a loose moistened dressing (moistened with sterile normal saline if available) and a first aid dressing over the tissue to protect it from further contamination. DO NOT remove or disturb any foreign matter that may be in the wound. Position the casualty so that their head is higher than their body. Keep them warm and seek medical assistance immediately.

review.notes: Confirmed: ATP 4-02.11 TBI signs, first-aid observable signs, CSF/blood leak, open head injury, symptoms can develop over time, most concussions without loss of consciousness, spinal precautions, nothing to eat or drink, no removal of protruding objects, open skull wound care; HHS (prolonged unconsciousness, evacuate; wake frequently; CNS-depressant pain medicine). Asks fit, including 'should I let him sleep' (A6). Conflict field is empty; I found no real disagreement: ATP 3-50.21 (awaken every 2 hours, monitor for 24 hours, cold pack on a bump) and WHO BEC agree, and HHS says withholding pain medication can be advised in head injury. No PDF junk. Recommended, not blocking: (1) ATP 3-50.21 says airway control is the most important part of head-injury care; a line such as 'if unconscious or vomiting, keep the airway clear (roll as one unit onto the side)' would answer 'bumped head now vomiting'; (2) the ATP 3-50.21 '24 hours / every 2 hours' figures would make A6 concrete.
